10.1002/mdr2.70073.scope: Reported multimodal design; diagnostic performance and clinical utility remain unverified.

sections.heading: Reported data and clinical task
sections.text: The paper describes an AI system for osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis and osteoporosis using routine laboratory measurements, demographics and symptom narratives. It reports 58,777 NHANES records, split into 49,523 training records from 1999–2016 and 9,254 temporal-test records from 2017–2018, plus 4,436 records from four Chinese centres. These are reported dataset roles, not independently verified evidence of clinical utility.
sections.source_locator: Results 2.1–2.2; Figure 3 caption

sections.heading: A specific, interpretable architecture
sections.text: The described fusion combines three structured-model scores with a 768-dimensional Bio_ClinicalBERT representation, producing 771 features for a classifier. The text encoder uses LoRA adapters; explicit diagnostic fields and disease names are described as removed or masked. This is a supervised prediction architecture with workflow orchestration, not evidence that a generative model independently reasons through diagnosis or improves patient outcomes.
sections.source_locator: Results 2.4 Multimodal Data Interconnection; Figure 5

sections.heading: Compare the multimodal training stages
sections.text: Section 2.4 provides a concrete stacking workflow for comparing structured and symptom-text models. It describes a multimodal comparison using hospitalization records from 126 patients at Shanghai Sixth People's Hospital. For fusion-head training, inner five-fold out-of-fold predictions supply the disease-specific structured scores. The structured models are then refitted on the full training set for validation and test scoring. After selection of the text-encoder checkpoint, the structured branch and LoRA-tuned text encoder remain fixed while a linear softmax fusion head is trained. These stages give a Methods comparison two specific checks: how predictions feeding the fusion model are generated, and which branch parameters are updated.
sections.source_locator: Results 2.4, paragraph specifying the two-stage stacking protocol and paragraph beginning Finally (126-patient multimodal comparison); Figure 5.

sections.heading: Performance claims remain limited
sections.text: All three printed training AUC estimates lie outside their accompanying confidence intervals. The 42-versus-41 predictor count and the relationship between test-set-based hyperparameter selection and later one-time evaluation also require clarification. The audit consequently does not endorse diagnostic accuracy, the reported multimodal improvement, or prospective self-screening effectiveness.
sections.source_locator: Results 2.2, Figure 2 caption and Figure 3C caption; Results 2.4

limitations: Training AUC/CI pairs are internally inconsistent.
Predictor count and model-selection/evaluation separation are unresolved.
Reported architecture does not demonstrate prospective clinical benefit.

sections.heading: Research question and data source
sections.text: This study examines multimorbidity and frailty using NHANES survey cycles from 1999–2018. sections.heading: Frailty definition and analysis
sections.text: Frailty is defined through a modified 36-item deficit-accumulation index. The Methods describe survey-weighted summaries and regression analyses. The authors report nested cross-validation with ten inner folds for hyperparameter tuning and five outer folds for model assessment. They compare six classifiers, including XGBoost, in Figure 4A (ROC) and Figure 4B (precision–recall). The complete item list, predictor overlap, leakage controls and independence of the evaluation cohort still require verification.

10.1177/00368504261499186.scope: Author-maintained explanation of an observational mortality analysis in CKM stages 0–3, supported by the indexed abstract and source-located reading of the published Methods.

sections.heading: Research question and design
sections.text: The study examined whether EASIX was associated with later mortality among 10,885 NHANES participants aged at least 30 years with cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome stages 0–3. It retrospectively analyzed survey cycles from 1999–2018, linking deaths through 2019. EASIX is calculated as lactate dehydrogenase multiplied by creatinine, divided by platelet count.
sections.source_locator: PubMed PMID 42893432, Abstract Objective and Methods: population, NHANES cycles, mortality linkage and EASIX definition.

sections.heading: Principal quantitative findings
sections.text: Over a median 97 months of follow-up, 1,122 participants died; 295 deaths were cardiovascular. Per one-unit higher EASIX, the adjusted hazard ratio was 1.41 (95% CI 1.24–1.61) for all-cause mortality and 1.30 (95% CI 1.13–1.49) for cardiovascular mortality. The abstract reports that the associations persisted after further lifestyle adjustment.
sections.source_locator: PubMed PMID 42893432, Abstract Results: follow-up, deaths, adjusted HRs and CIs, one-unit exposure scale and lifestyle adjustment.

sections.heading: Cohort and model specification
sections.text: Eligibility required a valid fasting-subsample weight and complete CKM-staging, EASIX, mortality-linkage and covariate information; participants were assigned their highest qualifying CKM stage, and stage 4 was excluded. Stage 3 included very-high-risk CKD or PREVENT 10-year total-CVD risk ≥20%; participants aged ≥80 years were assigned age 79 for PREVENT estimation. EASIX used LDH (U/L) × creatinine (mg/dL) / platelet count (10^9/L) and was modeled per one-unit increase and by quartiles. Analyses combined fasting-subsample weights with SDMVSTRA and SDMVPSU in survey-weighted Cox models. Model 2 added current smoking, BMI, systolic blood pressure, fasting glucose and antihypertensive, glucose-lowering and statin use to demographic adjustment. Follow-up ran from the baseline MEC examination to death or 31 December 2019; competing-risk analysis was a sensitivity analysis. These specifications support comparing cohort and model choices; the displayed Methods do not give the pooled-weight formula or exact cardiovascular-death codes.
sections.source_locator: Science Progress, published Methods Sections 2.1–2.5, covering cohort eligibility, CKM staging, EASIX, mortality linkage and statistical analysis.

sections.heading: Scientific contribution and publication context
sections.text: The analysis connects a composite endothelial-stress index with long-term outcomes among adults at CKM stages 0–3. It provides an observational comparator for epidemiologic discussions of endothelial stress, CKM staging and mortality; survey-weighted Cox models and spline analyses supply the reported association framework. Clinical risk-assessment use requires further validation. Electronic publication is recorded as 18 October 2026. The formal journal record is Science Progress, volume 109, issue 4 (2026), article 00368504261499186.
sections.source_locator: PubMed PMID 42893432, Abstract Methods and Conclusions: survey-weighted Cox models, restricted cubic splines, CKM stage scope and risk-assessment interpretation. PubMed ArticleDate DateType=Electronic 2026-10-18; Crossref volume 109, issue 4, article-number 00368504261499186 and published-print [2026,10].

limitations: The retrospective cohort associations support epidemiologic comparison; they do not establish that changing EASIX changes mortality or that EASIX is an externally validated clinical prediction model.

10.1016/j.gendis.2026.102480.scope: Author-maintained explanation of a published methodological review, based on the publisher's Journal Pre-proof in Cardiff University's repository and official bibliographic records.

sections.heading: Principal contribution
sections.text: This review connects biomedical data provenance and endpoint design with model selection, causal interpretation, validation, and deployment governance. Its disease-agnostic framework includes an evidence ladder for positioning AI findings and a proposed model-and-data card for reproducible reporting. It synthesizes methods across omics, imaging/pathology, clinical records, and longitudinal data to guide trustworthy research and translation.

sections.heading: Evidence ladder
sections.text: The review organizes support for an AI finding into association, robustness, biological coherence, causal support, perturbation evidence, and clinical utility. The ladder helps researchers identify what additional evidence is needed to move a finding toward a biological explanation or clinical application.
sections.source_locator: Evidence ladder, manuscript lines 491–518, physical PDF pages 26–27.

sections.heading: Research use
sections.text: The framework can inform the design and reporting of studies that combine biomedical data types. Its proposed model-and-data card gives researchers a place to document data provenance, model choices and validation conditions alongside the intended use.
sections.source_locator: Introduction, manuscript lines 121–133, physical PDF page 9; reporting and model-and-data card, lines 666–679, page 34.
